ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Sepsis after a sore throat

A previously healthy 19-year-old has recurrent high fever one week after a sore throat seemed to improve. He now has unilateral neck tenderness and pleuritic pain. CT shows internal jugular thrombosis and multiple peripheral cavitating lung nodules. Which syndrome is most likely?

  1. Lemierre syndrome
  2. Right-sided infective endocarditis
  3. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  4. Primary pulmonary tuberculosis
  5. Bland venous thromboembolism
Answer and explanation

Lemierre syndrome

Postpharyngeal sepsis with internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis and pulmonary septic emboli is characteristic of Lemierre syndrome.

Option explanations

Lemierre syndrome: Postpharyngeal sepsis with internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis and pulmonary septic emboli is characteristic of Lemierre syndrome.

Right-sided infective endocarditis: This may cause septic pulmonary emboli, but the postpharyngitis internal jugular thrombosis localizes the primary septic source to the neck.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: Cavitating lung nodules can occur, but septic jugular thrombosis after pharyngitis favors Lemierre syndrome.

Primary pulmonary tuberculosis: Tuberculosis does not explain this acute postpharyngitis septic thrombophlebitis pattern.

Bland venous thromboembolism: Bland emboli do not explain high fever and multiple septic-appearing cavitating nodules after a neck infection.
